comment: The architecture governs the stewardship of information models (SGI, LIMR) but does not standardise how models are made. Current artefact standards allow too many degrees of freedom: the same clinical concept can be modelled in many valid but incompatible ways, so two fully conformant implementations may still diverge semantically. A related, unnamed risk is the boundary problem: qualifiers, modifiers and localisations can be expressed in either the terminology or the information model, and this overlap breeds divergence.

public.text: The architecture governs the stewardship of information models (SGI, LIMR) but does not standardise how models are made. Current artefact standards allow too many degrees of freedom: the same clinical concept can be modelled in many valid but incompatible ways, so two fully conformant implementations may still diverge semantically. A related, unnamed risk is the boundary problem: qualifiers, modifiers and localisations can be expressed in either the terminology or the information model, and this overlap breeds divergence.
public.suggestedRevision: Require (in §3.4.5 and Appendix C) that artefacts in the LIMR be produced with a declared, uniform modelling method — one generic semantic pattern from which artefacts are derived by specialisation, with mandatory context (what, where, when, who, how, why) at capture — and test that meaning survives its application. The emerging CEN/ISO 13606 part 3 (SIAMM) work is one standards-track candidate; the requirement itself should remain method-neutral. Explicitly name — and assign governance responsibility for — the boundary problem between coding systems and information models.
